{{Short description|Family of three random counting measures}}

'''Poisson-type random measures''' are a family of three random [[counting measure]]s which are closed under restriction to a subspace, i.e. closed under thinning. They are the only distributions in the canonical non-negative [[power series]] family of distributions to possess this property and include the [[Poisson distribution]], [[negative binomial distribution]], and [[binomial distribution]].<ref>Caleb Bastian, Gregory Rempala. Throwing stones and collecting bones: Looking for Poisson-like random measures, Mathematical Methods in the Applied Sciences, 2020. [[doi:10.1002/mma.6224]]</ref> The PT family of distributions is also known as the Katz family of distributions,<ref>Katz L.. Classical and Contagious Discrete Distributions ch. Unified treatment of a broad class of discrete probability distributions, :175-182. Pergamon Press, Oxford 1965.</ref> the Panjer or [[(a,b,0) class of distributions]]<ref>Panjer Harry H.. Recursive Evaluation of a Family of Compound Distributions. 1981;12(1):22-26</ref> and may be retrieved through the [[Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution]].<ref>Conway R. W., Maxwell W. L.. A Queuing Model with State Dependent Service Rates. Journal of Industrial Engineering. 1962;12.</ref>

== Throwing stones ==
Let <math>K</math> be a non-negative integer-valued random variable <math>K\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}=\mathbb{N}_{>0}\cup\{0\}</math>) with law <math>\kappa</math>, mean <math>c\in(0,\infty)</math> and when it exists variance <math>\delta^2>0</math>. Let <math>\nu</math> be a probability measure on the [[measurable space]] <math>(E,\mathcal{E})</math>. Let <math>\mathbf{X}=\{X_i\}</math> be a collection of iid random variables (stones) taking values in <math>(E,\mathcal{E})</math> with law <math>\nu</math>.

The random counting measure <math>N</math> on <math>(E,\mathcal{E})</math> depends on the pair of deterministic probability measures <math>(\kappa,\nu)</math> through the '''stone throwing construction''' (STC) <ref>Cinlar Erhan. Probability and Stochastics. Springer-Verlag New York; 2011</ref>

<math>\quad N_\omega(A) = N(\omega,A) = \sum_{i=1}^{K(\omega)}\mathbb{I}_A(X_i(\omega))\quad \text{for} \quad\omega\in\Omega,\,\,\,A\in\mathcal{E}</math>

where <math>K</math> has law <math>\kappa</math> and iid <math>X_1,X_2,\dotsb</math> have law <math>\nu</math>. <math>N</math> is a [[mixed binomial process]]<ref>Kallenberg Olav. Random Measures, Theory and Applications. Springer; 2017</ref>

Let <math>\mathcal{E}_+=\{f: E\mapsto\mathbb{R}_+\}</math> be the collection of positive <math>\mathcal{E}</math>-measurable functions. The probability law of <math>N</math> is encoded in the '''[[Laplace functional]]'''

<math>\quad\mathbb{E} e^{-N f} =\mathbb{E} (\mathbb{E} e^{-f(X)})^K =\mathbb{E} (\nu e^{-f})^K=\psi(\nu e^{-f})\quad\text{for}\quad f\in\mathcal{E}_+</math>

where <math>\psi(\cdot)</math> is the generating function of <math>K</math>. The '''mean''' and '''variance''' are given by

<math>\quad\mathbb{E} Nf =c\nu f</math>

and

<math>\quad\mathbb{V}\text{ar} Nf = c\nu f^2 + (\delta^2-c) (\nu f)^2</math>

The '''covariance''' for arbitrary <math>f,g\in\mathcal{E}_+</math> is given by

<math>\quad\mathbb{C}\text{ov}(Nf,Ng) = c\nu(fg) + (\delta^2-c)\nu f \nu g</math>

When <math>K</math> is Poisson, negative binomial, or binomial, it is said to be '''Poisson-type''' (PT). The joint distribution of the collection <math>N(A),\ldots,N(B)</math> is for <math>i,\ldots, j \in \N</math> and <math>i+\cdots+j =k</math>

: <math>
\mathbb{P}(N(A)=i,\ldots, N(B)=j)=\mathbb{P}(N(A)=i,\ldots, N(B)=j|K=k)\,\mathbb{P}(K=k)=\frac{k!}{i!\cdots j!}\,\nu(A)^i\cdots \nu(B)^j\, \mathbb{P}(K=k)</math>

The following result extends construction  of a random measure <math>N=(\kappa,\nu)</math> to the case when the collection <math>\mathbf{X}</math> is expanded to <math>(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})=\{(X_i,Y_i)\}</math> where <math>Y_i</math> is a random transformation of <math>X_i</math>.  Heuristically, <math>Y_i</math> represents some properties (marks) of <math>X_i</math>. We assume that the conditional law of <math>Y</math> follows some [[transition kernel]] according to <math>\mathbb{P}(Y\in B|X=x)=Q(x,B)</math>.

=== Theorem: Marked STC ===
Consider random measure <math>N=(\kappa,\nu)</math> and the transition probability kernel <math>Q</math> from <math>(E, \cal E)</math> into <math>(F, \cal F)</math>.  Assume that given the collection <math>\mathbf{X}</math> the variables <math>\mathbf{Y}=\{Y_i\}</math> are [[Conditional independence|conditionally independent]] with <math>Y_i\sim Q(X_i,\cdot)</math>. Then <math>M=(\kappa, \nu\times Q)</math> is a random measure on <math>(E\times F, \cal E\otimes F)</math>. Here <math>\mu=\nu\times Q</math> is understood as <math>\mu(dx,dy)=\nu(dx)Q(x,dy)</math>. Moreover, for any <math>f\in ({\cal E}\otimes {\cal F})_+</math> we have that <math>\mathbb{E} e^{-M f}=\psi(\nu e^{-g})</math> where <math>\psi(\cdot )</math> is pgf of <math>K</math> and <math>g\in \mathcal{E}_+</math> is defined as  <math>e^{-g(x)}= \int_F Q(x,dy)e^{-f(x,y)}.</math>

The following corollary is an immediate consequence.

=== Corollary: Restricted STC ===
The quantity <math>N_A=(N\mathbb{I}_A,\nu_A)</math> is a well-defined random measure on the measurable subspace <math>(E\cap A, \mathcal{E}_A)</math> where <math>\mathcal{E}_A=\{A\cap B: B\in\mathcal{E}\}</math> and <math>\nu_A(B)=\nu(A\cap B)/\nu(A)</math>. Moreover, for any <math>f\in\mathcal{E}_+</math>, we have that <math>\mathbb{E} e^{-N_A f} = \psi(\nu e^{-f}\mathbb{I}_A+b)</math> where <math>b=1-\nu(A)</math>.

Note <math>\psi(\nu e^{-f}\mathbb{I}_A+1-a)=\psi_A(\nu_A e^{-f})</math> where we use <math>\nu e^{-f}\mathbb{I}_A=a\nu_A e^{-f}</math>.

== Collecting Bones ==
The probability law of the random measure is determined by its Laplace functional and hence generating function.

=== Definition: Bone ===
Let <math>K_A = N\mathbb{I}_A</math> be the counting variable of <math>K</math> restricted to <math>A\subset E</math>. When <math>\{N\mathbb{I}_A: A\subset E\}</math> and <math>K=N\mathbb{I}_E</math> share the same family of laws subject to a rescaling <math>h_a(\theta)</math> of the parameter <math>\theta</math>, then <math>K</math> is a called a '''bone''' distribution. The '''bone condition''' for the pgf is given by
<math>\psi_{\theta}(at+1-a)=\psi_{h_a(\theta)}(t)</math>.

Equipped with the notion of a bone distribution and condition, the main result for the existence and uniqueness of Poisson-type (PT) random counting measures is given as follows.

=== Theorem: existence and uniqueness of PT random measures ===

Assume that <math>K\sim \kappa_\theta</math> with pgf <math>\psi_\theta</math> belongs to the canonical non-negative power series (NNPS) family of distributions and <math>\{0,1\}\subset\text{supp}(K)</math>. Consider the random measure <math>N=(\kappa_\theta,\nu)</math> on the space <math>(E,\mathcal{E})</math> and assume that <math>\nu</math> is diffuse. Then for any <math>A\subset E</math> with <math>\nu(A)=a>0</math> there exists a mapping <math>h_a:\Theta\rightarrow\Theta</math> such that the restricted random measure is <math>N_A=(\kappa_{h_a(\theta)},\nu_A)</math>, that is,

<math>\quad \mathbb{E} e^{-N_A f} = \psi_{h_a(\theta)}(\nu_A e^{-f})\quad \text{for}\quad f\in\mathcal{E}_+</math>

iff <math>K</math> is Poisson, negative binomial, or binomial ('''Poisson-type''').

The proof for this theorem is based on a generalized additive Cauchy equation and its solutions. The theorem states that out of all NNPS distributions, only PT have the property that their restrictions <math>N\mathbb{I}_A</math> share the same family of distribution as <math>K</math>, that is, they are closed under thinning. The PT random measures are the [[Poisson random measure]], negative  binomial random measure, and binomial random measure. Poisson is '''additive''' with independence on disjoint sets, whereas negative binomial has positive covariance and binomial has negative covariance. The [[binomial process]] is a limiting case of binomial random measure where <math>p\rightarrow 1, n\rightarrow c</math>.

==Distributional self-similarity applications==

The "bone" condition on the pgf <math>\psi_\theta</math> of <math>K</math> encodes a distributional [[self-similarity]] property whereby all counts in restrictions (thinnings) to subspaces (encoded by pgf <math>\psi_A</math>) are in the same family as <math>\psi_\theta</math> of <math>K</math> through rescaling of the canonical parameter. These ideas appear closely connected to those of self-decomposability and stability of discrete random variables.<ref>Steutel FW, Van Harn K. Discrete analogues of self-decomposability and stability. The Annals of Probability. 1979;:893–899.</ref> Binomial thinning is a foundational model to count time-series.<ref>Al-Osh M. A., Alzaid A. A.. First-order integer-valued autoregressive (INAR(1)) process. Journal of Time Series Analysis. 1987;8(3):261–275.</ref><ref>Scotto Manuel G., Weiß Christian H., Gouveia Sónia. Thinning models in the analysis of integer-valued time series: a review. Statistical Modelling. 2015;15(6):590–618.</ref> The [[Poisson random measure]] has the well-known splitting property, is prototypical to the class of additive (completely random) random measures, and is related to the structure of [[Lévy processes]], the jumps of [[Kolmogorov equations (Markov jump process)|Kolmogorov equations]], and the excursions of [[Brownian motion]].<ref>Cinlar Erhan. Probability and Stochastics. Springer-Verlag New York; 2011.</ref> Hence the self-similarity property of the PT family is fundamental to multiple areas. The PT family members are "primitives" or prototypical random measures by which many random measures and processes can be constructed.
